lead: A basis is a list of vectors that is independent and spanning at the same time. Independence stops duplicates and hidden relations; spanning reaches every vector. Together they give each vector one coordinate list, like an address that cannot be written two ways. Engineers use coordinates to store, compress and solve. A photo is a list of numbers in a pixel basis; a UPI fraud model works on feature vectors in a chosen basis. The size of any basis is the dimension, a single number that tells you how much room the space has.
prereq: You need: linear combinations and span and linear dependence and independence.

blocks.text: A basis of a vector space V is a set B = {v₁, v₂, …, vₙ} of vectors in V with two properties. The set is independent: c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + ⋯ + cₙvₙ = 0 forces c₁ = c₂ = ⋯ = cₙ = 0. The set spans V: every vector v in V can be written as v = c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₙvₙ for some scalars c₁, …, cₙ. The scalars are real for a real space and complex for a complex space.

blocks.where: v is any vector in V; v₁, …, vₙ are the basis vectors; c₁, …, cₙ are the coordinates of v in that basis.

blocks.text: The two properties together make the list unique. If v = a₁v₁ + ⋯ + aₙvₙ and also v = b₁v₁ + ⋯ + bₙvₙ, subtract: (a₁ − b₁)v₁ + ⋯ + (aₙ − bₙ)vₙ = 0. Independence gives aᵢ − bᵢ = 0 for every i. So aᵢ = bᵢ.

A basis is a set; once we fix an order for its vectors we call it an ordered basis. For an ordered basis, the coordinate vector (c₁, …, cₙ) is unique. The ordered list (c₁, …, cₙ) is the coordinate vector of v in the basis B. The standard basis of Rⁿ is e₁ = (1, 0, …, 0), e₂ = (0, 1, 0, …, 0), …, eₙ = (0, …, 0, 1). The standard basis of Cⁿ over C is the same list. In R³, (2, −5, 7) = 2e₁ − 5e₂ + 7e₃, so its coordinates are (2, −5, 7).

Any two bases of the same finite-dimensional vector space have the same number of vectors. That common number is the dimension, written dim V. A space with a basis of n vectors has dimension n. The zero space {0} has empty basis and dim{0} = 0.

items: dim Rⁿ = n, because e₁, …, eₙ form a basis.
dim Cⁿ = n over C. Over R, Cⁿ has dimension 2n, since each complex coordinate needs a real and an imaginary part.
The polynomials of degree at most n, written Pₙ, have basis {1, t, t², …, tⁿ}. There are n + 1 vectors, so dim Pₙ = n + 1. The polynomial 4 − 3t + 2t² in P₂ has coordinates (4, −3, 2).
The space M_{m×n} of all m × n matrices has the matrix units E_{ij}. E_{ij} has 1 in row i and column j, and 0 everywhere else. There are mn such matrices, so dim M_{m×n} = mn.

blocks.text: The coordinate list of a vector in a basis of dimension n always has exactly n entries. Coordinates are written using an ordered basis, because swapping two basis vectors changes the coordinate list.

items: Any set of exactly n vectors taken from V is a basis if it spans V.
Any set of exactly n vectors taken from V is a basis if it is independent.

blocks.text: These rules save time in exams, but the count must be exact. n vectors that are dependent cannot span all of V, so they are not a basis. n + 1 vectors cannot be independent. A subspace W of a finite-dimensional space V has dim W ≤ dim V. Equality dim W = dim V happens only when W = V, so a proper subspace is always thinner.

Every spanning set contains a basis: throw away vectors that are combinations of the others until none is redundant. Every independent set sits inside a basis: add vectors until the set spans. The proofs are in the replacement theorem. A new basis changes coordinates; that is the change of basis used in Unit 3.

spec.title: Independence in R³
spec.aria: Three vectors in R³ that are independent must span the space, so they form a basis and the dimension is three.

examples.question: Is S = {(1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1), (1, 0, 1)} a basis of R³? Give the dimension.
steps: Write a(1, 1, 0) + b(0, 1, 1) + c(1, 0, 1) = (0, 0, 0), where a, b, c are real numbers.
Compare coordinates: a + c = 0, a + b = 0, b + c = 0.
From a + c = 0, c = −a. From a + b = 0, b = −a. Substitute in b + c = 0: (−a) + (−a) = −2a = 0, so a = 0. Then b = 0 and c = 0.
Only the zero combination gives the zero vector, so S is independent.
S has 3 vectors and dim R³ = 3. An independent set of 3 vectors in a 3-dimensional space is a basis. So S is a basis of R³.
examples.answer: S is a basis of R³; the coefficients are a = b = c = 0, and dim R³ = 3.
examples.check:
M = [[1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
     [1.0, 1.0, 0.0],
     [0.0, 1.0, 1.0]]
b = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
n = 3
for i in range(n):
    pivot = M[i][i]
    for j in range(i + 1, n):
        f = M[j][i] / pivot
        for k in range(i, n):
            M[j][k] -= f * M[i][k]
        b[j] -= f * b[i]
x = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
    s = b[i]
    for j in range(i + 1, n):
        s -= M[i][j] * x[j]
    x[i] = s / M[i][i]
for val in x:
    print(int(round(val)))
print(3)

traps: Thinking a basis must be orthogonal or must contain e₁, e₂, e₃. The set {(1, 1), (2, 1)} is a basis of R²: its determinant is 1×1 − 2×1 = −1 ≠ 0, it contains neither e₁ nor e₂, and (1, 1)·(2, 1) = 3 ≠ 0, so it is not orthogonal.
Calling every spanning set a basis. {e₁, e₂, e₁ + e₂} spans R² but is dependent, so it is not a basis.
Treating dimension as a property of a chosen list. R³ has dimension 3 even if you write down seven vectors from it.
Assuming any n vectors in an n-dimensional space form a basis. Three dependent vectors in R³ do not span R³.
Forgetting that coordinates depend on the ordered basis. Reordering the basis vectors reorders the coordinate list.

quiz.q: Define a basis of a vector space V.
quiz.a: A basis is a set of vectors in V that is both linearly independent and spans V.

quiz.q: What are dim R⁴ and dim P₃?
quiz.a: dim R⁴ = 4. P₃ has basis {1, t, t², t³}, so dim P₃ = 4.

quiz.q: Why does a basis give a unique coordinate list for every vector?
quiz.a: If one vector had two lists, subtracting the lists gives a combination of basis vectors equal to 0. Independence forces every coefficient in that difference to be 0, so the two lists are the same.
The only vector in {0} is 0. The empty set spans {0} and is independent, so it is a basis with 0 vectors.

quiz.q: Is S = {(1, 2), (3, 4)} a basis of R²?
quiz.a: Form the matrix with these vectors as columns: [[1, 3], [2, 4]]. Its determinant is 1×4 − 3×2 = −2, which is not 0. The two vectors are independent, and R² has dimension 2, so S is a basis.

quiz.q: Can four vectors in R³ be independent? Can three dependent vectors span R³?
quiz.a: No to both. Four vectors in a 3-dimensional space must be dependent. Three dependent vectors span a subspace of dimension at most 2, not all of R³.

quiz.q: V has dim 5. W is a subspace with dim 4. Can W = V? Can an independent set of 4 vectors in V span V?
quiz.a: No to both. dim W = 4 < 5 = dim V, so W is a proper subspace. Four independent vectors span a 4-dimensional subspace, not the 5-dimensional V.

quiz.q: In R³, S has 4 vectors and spans R³. Must S be a basis? Does S contain a basis?
quiz.a: S is not a basis because a basis of R³ has exactly 3 vectors. Since S spans R³, it contains a basis: remove one redundant vector and the remaining 3 span R³.

beyond: Not for the exam. Basis choice is the heart of compression: JPEG uses a cosine basis, and PCA picks a data-driven basis. Numerical libraries prefer orthonormal bases because coordinates are stable under rounding; see Unit 5. In machine learning, feature maps send data into high-dimensional spaces where a basis describes the features. Search 'change of basis', 'orthonormal basis', and 'rank-nullity theorem'.
